Orator

OR-uh-tur -- from Latin orare, 'to speak, to plead,' from os, 'mouth': an orator speaks with the whole force of the mouth. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Orator is a skilled public speaker.

Frederick Douglass was such a powerful orator that audiences often fell completely silent within the first minute of his speeches.

Worked Example

Though she had never given a speech before, the exchange student stood at the podium and spoke so clearly and persuasively about her home country that the entire cafeteria stopped eating to listen.

An orator doesn't need years of formal training -- what matters is the ability to speak clearly and persuasively enough to hold a room's attention, exactly what the exchange student did on her very first try.

How Orator Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

speaker

speaker: someone who speaks, especially in public

rhetorician

rhetorician: someone skilled in persuasive speaking technique

Antonyms

listener

listener: someone who listens rather than speaks

wallflower

wallflower: a shy person who avoids public attention

How Strong Is It? — speaker → orator → rhetorician

speaker vs. orator

speaker vs. orator: Speaker is the plain, everyday word for anyone who talks in public, skilled or not -- calling someone an orator specifically praises their skill.

rhetorician vs. orator

rhetorician vs. orator: Rhetorician goes further than orator -- it emphasizes deliberate technique and persuasive craft, almost like a scholar of speech, while orator can simply mean someone who speaks powerfully.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — or-

root — or-: mouth, to speak (Latin orare, from os ('mouth'))

suffix — -ator

suffix — -ator: one who does an action (Latin -ator)

Put it together

Put it together: Orator comes from Latin orare, 'to speak or plead,' itself from os, 'mouth' -- an orator is literally 'one who speaks,' the same root that gives us oral and oration.
